node.label: Londa Schiebinger
node.date_label: The Mind Has No Sex? (1989) · Nature’s Body (1993) · Plants and Empire (2004) · Secret Cures of Slaves (2017)
node.description: In The Mind Has No Sex? (1989), Londa Schiebinger argued that women’s exclusion from scientific institutions and scientific accounts of female incapacity reinforced one another. Nature’s Body (1993) extended this analysis to show how assumptions about gender and race shaped scientific explanations of nature. She distinguishes women’s participation, scientific institutions and the content of knowledge as connected historical problems. Plants and Empire (2004) investigates selective knowledge transfer in colonial settings; Secret Cures of Slaves (2017) examines medicine and experimentation in the Atlantic world. Nature’s Body received the Society for Social Studies of Science’s Ludwik Fleck Book Prize in 1995. Michael Stolberg’s “A Woman Down to Her Bones” (2003) argued that physicians around 1600 already emphasised and illustrated distinct features of the female skeleton, challenging the eighteenth-century chronology she shared with Laqueur. In “Skelettestreit” (2003) Schiebinger replied that such early depictions were isolated, that female-sexed skeletons became widespread only after about 1730, and that foundational shifts should not be judged by firsts.

proposed_edges.relationship: In 'The Philosopher's Beard' (2003), Schiebinger draws on Shapin's A Social History of Truth (1994) to explain how women in seventeenth-century England lacked standing in the economy of civility that guaranteed experimental truth, with Boyle as the ideal 'modest witness'.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher PDF of “The Philosopher’s Beard” (2003), printed p. 195 (PDF leaf 12), paragraph beginning Other scholars have located the gendering of science, and n. 25. The body summarizes and uses Shapin’s account of women’s lack of standing in the economy of civility that guaranteed experimental truth; the following sentence identifies Boyle as the ideal modest witness. Note 25 cites A Social History of Truth (1994). This replaces the stale locator for a different chapter. Shapin’s book remains unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: The Mind Has No Sex? (1989) connected women’s institutional exclusion with the gendering of scientific knowledge, a programme Schiebinger described in her 2024 Cell interview.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Interview, first answer, paragraphs beginning “When I began the project” and “Beginning with my doctoral dissertation.” Author’s retrospective; book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: The Mind Has No Sex? (1989) recovered women’s scientific activity that histories of the scientific revolution had overlooked.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Interview, first answer, paragraph beginning “The deciding point came around 1981.” Claim limited to the research intervention described by the author.

proposed_edges.relationship: Nature’s Body (1993) examines how assumptions about gender, sex and race shaped scientific explanations of nature.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Rutgers publisher description, final paragraph, and contents; “assumptions about gender, sex, and race.” Description only; 2004 reissue distinguished from 1993 original.

proposed_edges.relationship: “Feminist History of Colonial Science” (2004) brings gender analysis to selective collecting and unequal knowledge transfer between Europe and its colonies.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher abstract, first two sentences: “selective collecting practices.” Editorial contribution to the imperial-knowledge field; no claimed debt to Said or Spivak. Article body unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: “Medical Experimentation and Race in the Eighteenth-century Atlantic World” (2013) studies the tension between racial differentiation and assumptions of interchangeable bodies in medical trials.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher abstract, sentences 3–6: “required that human bodies be fully interchangeable.” Abstract only; no generalization to all experiments or periods.

proposed_edges.relationship: In his H-Atlantic review (2006) of Plants and Empire (2004), McNeill found the book's central argument, that knowledge of the peacock flower's abortifacient use did not travel from the Caribbean to Europe, 'interesting if not ... altogether convincing', and judged its conclusion not fully consistent with its earlier denial that the knowledge was suppressed.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the complete review (10 paragraphs), John R. McNeill, 'One Plant and Several Scientists', H-Atlantic, H-Net Reviews, February 2006, in an Internet Archive capture of the H-Net page (capture 20150920135053) held in the project's H-Net review corpus; the live H-Net page returned 403 to the fetch tool. Paragraph 5 ('Among those abortifacients...'): 'I hoped for more explanation of that fact than the chapter provided.' Paragraph 7 ('In the conclusion (chapter 6)...'): the hypotheses are 'interesting and plausible, but not fully consonant with this earlier position', citing Schiebinger pp. 153 and 238. Paragraph 8 ('Of course, there may have been other inhibitions...') offers an alternative explanation (cost of a tropical plant, other abortion methods) and labels it 'a mere hypothesis'. Paragraph 10 ('This is a work in the history of science...'): 'makes an interesting if not, to my mind, altogether convincing case'. The review also praises the book ('an entertaining book that raises some interesting questions', paragraph 1). Plants and Empire itself unread; the edge records McNeill's assessment only.

proposed_edges.relationship: In 'The Philosopher's Beard' (2003), Schiebinger describes the eighteenth-century revolution in sexual science as marked by what Laqueur, in Making Sex (1990), called a shift from a one-sex to a two-sex model of difference, and points readers to Park and Nye's critical evaluation of his work.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher PDF of the chapter (Cambridge History of Science, vol. 4, pp. 184-210). Body text, section 'The Science of Woman', PDF p. 14 (printed p. 197, inferred from the file's page range because the PDF's numerals do not extract): 'The revolution in sexual science was also marked by what Thomas Laqueur has described as a shift from a one-sex to a two-sex model of difference.' The following paragraph sets out the two models in her own words. Note 34 (printed p. 198) cites Making Sex and adds 'See also the critical evaluation of Laqueur's work by Katharine Park and Robert Nye'. This is body-text adoption of Laqueur's framework, not a footnote citation. Independently, Michael Stolberg's author abstract (Isis 94, 2003, read at PubMed 12879558) treats the claim as 'Thomas Laqueur's and Londa Schiebinger's influential claim'; that pairing corroborates the shared position but is not used as the basis of this edge. Making Sex itself unread. The held ls_w_03 (Laqueur drew on Schiebinger, the opposite direction) remains unverified and is not restored.

proposed_edges.relationship: In 'The Philosopher's Beard' (2003), Schiebinger presents Merchant's The Death of Nature (1980) as a classic explanation of the gendering of science and holds that Merchant 'rightly called attention' to the gendering of nature as female, while noting the criticism that the book reinforced the association of women with nature.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher PDF, section '"Learned Venuses," "Austere Minervas," and "Homosocial Brotherhoods"', PDF p. 10 (printed p. 193, inferred from the file's page range), paragraph beginning 'Scholars have explained the gendering of science in different ways': 'In her classic [1980] Death of Nature, Carolyn Merchant revealed how the rise of a mechanistic worldview entailed the "death of nature."' The paragraph summarises Merchant's argument about Bacon's rhetoric and closes: 'Although roundly criticized for reinforcing the traditional notion that women belong to nature in ways that men do not, Merchant rightly called attention to the adamant gendering of nature as female in both ancient and modern science traditions.' Note 22 cites The Death of Nature. The year numeral does not extract from the PDF text layer; 1980 is the book's known original date and matches the graph's Merchant node. This answers the earlier held lead (Signs 2003 introduction unread) with a different, read passage. The Death of Nature itself unread here.

proposed_edges.relationship: Schiebinger's Gendered Innovations project (begun 2009) extended sex and gender analysis in research design to intersectional analysis, crediting the term to Crenshaw (1989), as she explains in her 2024 Cell interview.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Stanford History reprint of the Cell Q&A (14 March 2024), already the source of ls_w_04. Answer to 'What is "Gendered Innovations?"': 'In 2009, when we started, "Gendered Innovations" was the right term; we have now expanded to include intersectional innovations', and the project's goal is 'to provide scientists and engineers with practical methods for sex, gender, and intersectional analysis.' Answer to 'What about intersectional analyses?': 'The term was coined in 1989 by legal scholar Kimberle Crenshaw', followed by the Gender Shades example; 'It's the intersectional analysis that most interests me'. Answer on journals: 'A group of us are now working on producing a similar set of author and editor guidelines for intersectionality.' Retrospective self-account of a current project; Gendered Innovations publications not separately read. Applies intersectional analysis to science and engineering research; no claim that she shaped the concept itself.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Secret Cures of Slaves: People, Plants, and Medicine in the Eighteenth-Century Atlantic World (2017), Schiebinger contributes to Atlantic history by reconstructing medical knowledge’s circulation and obstruction within the Caribbean and between the Caribbean, Europe and West Africa, as Helen Bynum’s review explains.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Bynum’s complete review on the journal publisher’s site. It describes an integrated account of Atlantic medical exchange and maps showing its direction and interruptions. The field contribution is supported through this review; the book itself remains unread. No claim about particular transmitted remedies is proposed.
